newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian bonds back track on data, no rout.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian bonds back track on data, no rout.

text.p: FUTURES CASH YIELD
*Australian bond yields finished higher after stronger than expected capital expenditure data for the third quarter thwarted hopes of an imminent cut in domestic interest rates.
*However, bill futures still point to a cut next year
By Colin Brinsden
Australian bond prices retreated as hopes of an imminent cut in interest rates were thwarted by a stronger than expected third quarter capital expenditure report.
"A Reserve Bank interest rate cut in December now seems out of the question," said Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura Research Australia.

However, while yields were above the day's initial lows, the debt market did not succumb to a selling rout on the data, and March bill futures were still predicting a 25 basis point monetary policy easing in the first quarter next year.

Capital expenditure rose 0.9 percent compared with a median forecast for a 3.0 percent fall, but more importantly, the fourth estimate for business investment intentions for 1996/97 rose by 7.8 percent over the third estimate.

Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said the September quarter data showed that the government's August budget forecast of 14 percent growth in business investment for 1996/97 would be met, a point that no economist disagreed on.
"If the economy is still running well, further gains in bond markets seem difficult," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank.

"It will take more bad news on the economy or leads from overseas to push yields down," Kunnen said, but added that there was still overwhelming evidence that the economy remains soft and he still expected a further rate cut next year.

Nomura's Pease also saw a chance of a policy easing next year, but this would depend even more on the outlook for wages. "Any future interest rate cut will be as a reward for continuing low inflation and moderation in wages demands," he said.
However, Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia, felt that Monday's data all but killed the chances for a rate cut before March 1997.

"As such, the bond market rally is close to running its full course," he said. "While the flow of funds from yield hungry offshore investors could limit the extent of any sell off, on domestic fundamentals there is scope for yields to back up."

The benchmark 10-year bond again came within a whisker of making a clean break of 7.0 percent before the data, while the December 10-year bond futures contract matched Friday's 92.995 33-month peak, but quickly went into reverse after it.
March bill futures also eased from a contract high of 93.92, but at its closing 93.85 it was pointing to a cash rate of 6.15 percent compared with current 6.50 percent official rates.
AUD VS 3-YR 10-YR * AUD 3-YR/10-YR SPREAD

The local market's retracement saw it reverse an initial tightening trend to other dollar bloc bond yields. The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread briefly broke resistance at 90 basis points before the Capex report.

The 10-year bond contract retraced through a support area between 92.950 to 92.920 after again being knocked back from 92.995. Solid support seen at 92.845 on any further fall. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
